title: Nanak's teachings close
hookLine: a dialogue, an alphabet, a lament, the months, and three pillars

lines: A MOUNTAIN, AN ALPHABET, A LAMENT.
cards: Suppose you could keep one sentence from the last several weeks, and only one. A circle of yogis on a mountain asking a stranger who he is. A pandit's alphabet turned into a poem.
A child's writing tablet, one letter at a time. A lament for a city attacked and the women who suffered there. A year of months, each one aching.
A ballad that holds every name up against a life. Three short phrases about remembering, working and sharing. That's a lot of road.
Today, a look back down it.

teach.b: Lay the pieces side by side and one move keeps repeating: Guru Nanak takes something outward and turns it inward, without throwing it away.
In the Sidh Gosht, the yogis wear earrings and a patched coat; he makes the Word the earring, worn within, and turns the coat into seeing the One in everything.

In the Oankar, a learned man reads and argues; Nanak asks whether he has understood, and calls true learning reflection on the Name. In the Patti, a school slate becomes a lesson for the soul, one letter at a time.
In the Babarvani, faith doesn't look away; it names the pain of ordinary people caught in an invasion. In his twelve months in Raga Tukhari, every season becomes a way of longing for the Beloved.
In the Var in Majh, a name becomes a promise to live up to. And in the three phrases, a job, a meal and a breath each become practice. So that is Nanak's way, as these weeks have shown it.
Living in it like a lotus in water, untouched, and making every ordinary thing point somewhere. One more detail before new ground. Guru Nanak's hymns are signed with his name, Nanak.
The Gurus whose hymns follow his in the Granth signed them Nanak too, and a heading tells you whose voice it is: Mahala one, Mahala two, and on.
The name carries on into the next voice.

how: Sikhs meet Guru Nanak's longer compositions, such as the Sidh Gosht, Oankar, Patti and Barah Maha, in kirtan and in katha at the gurdwara, sometimes studied over a run of sessions.

o: a look back: outward things turned inward, in the world
the last hymn Guru Nanak wrote before he died
the end of Nanak's travels, back home in Punjab

games.q: the teaching and what it turned inward: tap the pairs.
p: a school slate becomes a soul's lesson

s: the Gurus whose hymns follow his in the Granth also signed them Nanak
a heading, Mahala one, Mahala two and on, tells whose voice it is.
in the Babarvani, Nanak looks away from the suffering of the invasion
he names the pain of ordinary people and mourns them.
Nanak's way, in these teachings, means leaving the world behind
it means living in it like a lotus in water and turning ordinary things inward.

games.q: the yogis in the Sidh Gosht wear earrings and a patched coat as signs of their path. what does Nanak say?
o: take them off; they mean nothing.
the Word is the earring, worn within.
games.why: he doesn't mock the signs; he turns them inward: the Guru's Word as the earring, worn where no one sees it.

practice: Let the stretch pass by again, the mountain conversation, the alphabet, the tablet, the lament, the months, the ballad, the three phrases, and don't choose the one that sounds wisest.
Notice which one keeps coming back to you, and hold it on the breath for a while. If you pray, say Waheguru quietly on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Nanak's teachings close. A dialogue, an alphabet, a lament, the months, a ballad and three pillars, all turning the outward world inward. Today's word.

orig.note: the name that signs Guru Nanak's hymns, and the hymns of the Gurus after him.

carryVoice: Your line: nanak's way. Next comes the voice that carried his name on. Until tomorrow.
